title: Merehall
subtitle: Seat of House Northmere
content:
**Merehall** is the seat of [[House Northmere]], situated on the shores of the great northern lake.

## Architecture
A sprawling, low-built hall of grey stone, more longhouse than castle. The original structure dates back centuries, with additions built as needed rather than planned. Docks extend into the lake where fishing boats tie up.

## Surroundings
The great lake dominates the landscape - cold, deep, and rich with fish. Peat bogs stretch inland, providing fuel for the north. The Northmeres have fished these waters since before anyone kept records.

## Notable Features
- The Long Dock: Where the fishing fleet moors
- The Smoke House: Ancient structure for preserving fish
- The Peat Stores: Vast covered yards of drying peat

title: Wardkeep
subtitle: Seat of House Kingsward
content:
**Wardkeep** is the seat of [[House Kingsward]], a fortified garrison on the northern royal road.

## Architecture
A functional military fortress rather than a lordly castle. Square towers, thick walls, and a large gatehouse spanning the road. Designed to control passage, not to impress.

## Surroundings
Wardkeep straddles the northern royal road at a natural chokepoint between hills. All traffic north or south must pass through its gates and pay its tolls.

## Notable Features
- The King's Gate: Main passage through, tolls collected here
- The Garrison Yard: Barracks for Crown soldiers
- The Road Tower: Watchtower with views for miles in each direction

title: Granford Keep
subtitle: Seat of House Granford
content:
**Granford Keep** is the seat of [[House Granford]], surrounded by the richest farmland in the Northern Crown Marches.

## Architecture
A practical, well-maintained keep with extensive outbuildings - barns, granaries, and cattle sheds. The Granfords invest in their farms, not their walls.

## Surroundings
Rolling fields of wheat, barley, and oats stretch to the horizon. Fat cattle graze in meadows. This is the breadbasket of the north - modest by southern standards, but vital up here.

## Notable Features
- The Great Granary: Stores enough grain to feed the northern houses through hard winters
- The Cattle Fair: Annual market drawing buyers from across the region
- The Mill: Water-powered, grinding grain for the whole district

title: Moorstead
subtitle: Seat of House Croftmoor
content:
**Moorstead** is the seat of [[House Croftmoor]], a remote stronghold on the edge of the northern moors.

## Architecture
A squat, weathered tower surrounded by a low wall - built to endure harsh conditions rather than siege. Outbuildings cluster close for protection from the wind.

## Surroundings
Endless moorland stretches in all directions - heather, gorse, and rough grass. Sheep dot the landscape. The wind never stops. It is beautiful in a bleak way, and deeply isolated.

## Notable Features
- The Herb Garden: Walled enclosure where moorland medicinals are cultivated
- The Sheep Folds: Stone enclosures dotting the moors for miles
- The Signal Tower: For communicating across the vast moorland distances

title: Helm Castle
subtitle: Seat of House Helmward
content:
**Helm Castle** is the seat of [[House Helmward]], a border fortress in the northern marches.

## Architecture
A true military castle - high walls, strong towers, and a well-designed killing ground before the gates. The Helmwards have defended this border for generations and their home reflects it.

## Surroundings
Rocky, defensible terrain on the edge of settled lands. Beyond lies wilderness - and whatever threats emerge from it. The castle watches the passes and guards the approaches.

## Notable Features
- The Armoury: One of the finest collections of weapons in the north
- The Training Yard: Where every Helmward child learns the sword
- The Watch Fires: Beacon system to warn of approaching threats

title: Blackmoor Hall
subtitle: Seat of House Blackmoor
content:
**Blackmoor Hall** is the seat of [[House Blackmoor]], rising from the dark peatlands of the northern bogs.

## Architecture
An ancient hall built on an island of solid ground amid the bogs. Dark stone, small windows, and a perpetual smell of peat smoke. The approach is treacherous to those who don't know the paths.

## Surroundings
Black water, dark peat, and grey mist. The bogs are dangerous but productive - peat for fuel, bog iron for smithing, eels for eating. The Blackmoors know every safe path; outsiders frequently don't.

## Notable Features
- The Bog Paths: Secret routes known only to the family and trusted servants
- The Iron Pits: Where bog iron is harvested and smelted
- The Old Shrine: Ancient stones predating the hall, still honored with offerings

title: Cresthold
subtitle: Seat of House Stormcrest
content:
**Cresthold** is the seat of [[House Stormcrest]], perched on cliffs overlooking the northern sea.

## Architecture
A windswept castle built into the cliff face, with a protected harbor below. Salt-stained stone and iron-bound doors that can withstand the worst storms. Ships are as important as walls here.

## Surroundings
The northern sea - grey, cold, and full of fish. Rocky coastline with hidden coves. The Stormcrests know every inlet and current along this stretch of coast.

## Notable Features
- The Harbor: Protected anchorage carved from the cliff base
- The Salt Works: Where sea water is evaporated for salt
- The Trader's Hall: Where goods from distant ports are bought and sold

title: Thornwick Manor
subtitle: Seat of House Thornwick
content:
**Thornwick Manor** is the seat of [[House Thornwick]], the newest of the Northern Crown Houses.

## Architecture
A comfortable manor house rather than a castle - the Thornwicks were elevated to nobility only three generations ago and their home reflects their origins as wealthy farmers. Well-built but unpretentious.

## Surroundings
Good farmland, some woodland, a village of tenants. Nothing remarkable, but solid and productive. The Thornwicks are still building their legacy.

## Notable Features
- The New Hall: Recently expanded great hall, eager to host important guests
- The Orchards: Apple and pear trees, a point of pride
- The Village: Prosperous tenants who remember when the Thornwicks were just farmers like them

title: Ashford Hall
subtitle: Seat of House Ashford
content:
**Ashford Hall** is the seat of [[House Ashford]], a modest manor near a river crossing.

## Architecture
A comfortable old hall, neither grand nor decrepit. The Ashfords have held this land for centuries, maintaining it without expanding it. The hall looks much as it did generations ago.

## Surroundings
Mixed farmland along a small river. An old stone bridge gives the place its name - "ash ford" from the ash trees that once lined the crossing. Pleasant, unremarkable country.

## Notable Features
- The Old Bridge: Stone crossing that has stood for centuries
- The Ash Grove: Replanted after the original trees died, maintaining tradition
- The Family Chapel: Small but ancient, with Ashford tombs dating back generations

title: Fenwick Keep
subtitle: Seat of House Fenwick
content:
**Fenwick Keep** is the seat of [[House Fenwick]], an ancient tower in the northern forests.

## Architecture
A single tall tower of old stone, surrounded by wooden outbuildings. The keep predates written records - the Fenwicks claim it was ancient when their ancestors first held it. It has been repaired but never expanded.

## Surroundings
Dense forest - oak, ash, and pine. Hunting grounds that have provided for the Fenwicks for longer than anyone remembers. The trees press close, and the keep feels hidden from the world.

## Notable Features
- The Ancient Tower: Original structure of unknown age
- The Hunting Lodge: Deep in the forest, where the lords stay during long hunts
- The Fur Store: Where pelts are prepared for trade

title: Grantholm
subtitle: Seat of House Wilson
content:
**Grantholm** is the seat of [[House Wilson]], located in the [[Northern Crown Marches]] approximately two weeks' ride from [[Breakmount Castle]].

## The Northern Crown Marches

Grantholm lies within lands held directly by the Crown — territory administered by royal officers rather than any Wilfrey Drith. This placement was deliberate: the king granted Lennis and Nivette lands where they would be neighbors to loyal Crown houses ([[House Northmere]], [[House Kingsward]], [[House Granford]], etc.) rather than Wilfrey vassals.

## Origin

The castle and surrounding lands were granted by royal charter ~1778, with formal Crown recognition of House Wilson in 1785. The king welcomed [[Lennis Wilfrey]] and [[Nivette Wilfson]] after their exile, giving them a place beyond Wilfrey authority where their marriage could not be challenged.

## Architecture

Unlike the great castles of the four Wilfrey seats, Grantholm is modest but well-built. The original structure was small — little more than a fortified manor granted from an extinct line. Each generation has added to it, but the Wilsons have never sought to rival the grandeur of [[Breakmount Castle]] or [[Fourhearth Castle]].

## Economy

The surrounding lands produce:
- Sheep (wool trade)
- Grain (wheat and barley)
- Some forestry

The wealth is modest but steady. House Wilson has never been rich, but they have never been poor either. Their northern neighbors — the Crown Houses — are their primary trading partners and marriage allies.

## The Grant

The name "Grantholm" reflects the royal grant that established it. Some say the founders chose the name deliberately — a constant reminder that their house exists by the king's grace, not the Wilfrey council's permission.

## See Also
- [[House Wilson]]: The house seated here
- [[Lennis Wilfrey]]: Founder who received the grant
- [[Northern Crown Marches]]: The region where Grantholm sits
- [[Breakmount Castle]]: The Wilfrey principal seat, two weeks' ride south

title: Northern Crown Marches
subtitle: Crown Lands Beyond Wilfrey Authority
content:
**The Northern Crown Marches** are a region of the kingdom held directly by the Crown, lying beyond the traditional Wilfrey sphere of influence. Approximately two weeks' ride north of [[Breakmount Castle]], these lands are administered by royal officers rather than any Wilfrey Drith.

## Character

The Northern Crown Marches are rugged, remote, and independent. The land is poorer than the Wilfrey heartland — more moorland than meadow, more sheep than cattle — but the people who live here are proud of their self-sufficiency.

## The Northern Crown Houses

Ten minor houses hold lands directly from the Crown in this region, forming a loose network of families who:
1. Hold lands directly from the Crown (not through any Wilfrey intermediary)
2. Intermarry primarily among themselves and with [[House Wilson]]
3. Maintain cordial but distant relations with Wilfrey territory
4. Share a common identity as "northerners" distinct from the Wilfrey web

These houses are: [[House Northmere]], [[House Kingsward]], [[House Granford]], [[House Croftmoor]], [[House Helmward]], [[House Blackmoor]], [[House Stormcrest]], [[House Thornwick]], [[House Ashford]], and [[House Fenwick]].

## House Wilson

[[House Wilson]], despite its Wilfrey blood, is accepted as part of this northern network due to the royal grant that established them outside Wilfrey authority. Over 250 years, they have become deeply integrated through marriage alliances with all ten Northern Crown Houses.

## See Also
- [[Grantholm]]: Seat of House Wilson
- [[House Wilson]]: The broken branch at the heart of the network

title: The Baudin Tradition
subtitle: We Remember Baudin — The Wilson Naming Custom
content:
**The Baudin Tradition** is the custom of [[House Wilson]] whereby every firstborn son is named Baudin (or a variant), honoring [[Baudin Wilfson]] — the fostering brother who died defending the founders' marriage.

## Origin

When [[Lennis Wilfrey]] and [[Nivette Wilfson]] fled north after [[The Scandal of 1776]], Baudin Wilfson — Nivette's brother — had just been killed by their younger brother [[Colard Wilfson]] for defending their union. The founders named their firstborn son Baudin. The name was deliberate and defiant — honoring the brother who gave his life.

## Purpose

The practice serves multiple purposes:
1. **Memory**: Ensures Baudin Wilfson is never forgotten
2. **Identity**: Distinguishes Wilsons from other houses
3. **Defiance**: A constant reminder that they exist because someone chose love over duty
4. **Healing**: Transforms a tragedy into a blessing — "Baudin gave his life so we could live"

## The Line of Baudins

| Generation | Name | Born | Died |
|-----------|------|------|------|
| 1 | Baudin Wilson I | ~1778 | ~1850 |
| 2 | Baudin Wilson II | ~1802 | ~1875 |
| 3 | Baudin Wilson III | ~1830 | ~1905 |
| 4 | Baudin Wilson IV | ~1858 | ~1935 |
| 5 | Baudin Wilson V | ~1888 | ~1965 |
| 6 | Baudin Wilson VI | ~1920 | ~1995 |
| 7 | Baudin Wilson VII | ~1950 | living |
| 8 | Baudin Wilson VIII | ~1978 | living |
| 9 | Baudin Wilson IX | ~2007 | living |

## Contrast with House Wilfson

Interestingly, [[House Wilfson]] — the house that remained after the kinslaying — also kept Baudin's memory through naming variants: Baudric, Bauric, and eventually the full name Baudin reclaimed 250 years later. The two houses, separated by exile, independently honored the same man through the same practice.

## The Response

When asked about the naming tradition, Wilsons typically respond: "We remember Baudin. We always will."

## See Also
- [[Baudin Wilfson]]: The original Baudin
- [[House Wilson]]: The house that keeps the tradition
- [[The Scandal of 1776]]: The tragedy that inspired it
- [[Lennis Wilfrey]]: Who named the first Baudin Wilson
- [[Nivette Wilfson]]: Baudin's sister, co-founder of House Wilson

title: Baudin Wilson VII
subtitle: Eighth Lord of House Wilson — The Current Lord
content:
**Baudin Wilson VII** (b. ~1950) is the current and eighth Lord of [[House Wilson]], having succeeded his father [[Baudin Wilson VI]] in ~1995. He is the eighth generation to bear the name Baudin, continuing the tradition established when the founders named their firstborn for [[Baudin Wilfson]].

## The Current Lord

Baudin VII has led House Wilson through the modern era, maintaining the family's position in the [[Northern Crown Marches]] and its network of alliances with the Northern Crown Houses.

## Marriage to House Stormcrest

Baudin VII married Eveline of [[House Stormcrest]] (~1975), a seafaring Northern Crown House seated at [[Cresthold]]. Their daughter Evelind later married Garrett Stormcrest (~2005), creating a double bond.

## Children

- [[Baudin Wilson VIII]] (b. ~1978) — heir, married Marelisse of [[House Thornwick]]
- Evelind Stormcrest (b. ~1982) — daughter, married Garrett Stormcrest
- Lenric Wilson (b. ~1985) — son, named to honor founder [[Lennis Wilfrey]]

## The Tradition's Weight

When asked about the naming tradition, Wilsons typically respond: "We remember Baudin. We always will." Baudin VII embodies this — a steady lord carrying 250 years of family memory.

subtitle: Heir to House Wilson
content:
**Baudin Wilson VIII** (b. ~1978) is the heir to [[House Wilson]], eldest son of [[Baudin Wilson VII]] and Eveline Stormcrest. He is the ninth generation to bear the name Baudin.

## Marriage to House Thornwick

Baudin VIII married Marelisse of [[House Thornwick]] (~2005), the youngest of the Northern Crown Houses (founded ~1920). This match elevated House Thornwick's status considerably — marriage to the Wilson heir was a significant honor for a house only three generations old.

## Children

- Baudin Wilson IX (b. ~2007) — heir, tenth generation to bear the name
- Marelle Wilson (b. ~2010) — daughter, too young to marry

## The Name Continues

With Baudin IX, the tradition stretches to its tenth generation. The name that began as a defiant memorial — honoring [[Baudin Wilfson]] who died in [[The Scandal of 1776]] — has become the defining characteristic of House Wilson's identity.

title: Baudin Wilson I
subtitle: Second Lord — First Born a Wilson
content:
**Baudin Wilson I** (~1778-~1850) was the second Lord of [[House Wilson]], ruling from ~1815 to ~1850. He was the first child born to [[Lennis Wilfrey]] and [[Nivette Wilfson]] after their settlement at [[Grantholm]], and the first person to bear the name Baudin Wilson.

## The Name

His parents named him for [[Baudin Wilfson]] — Nivette's brother who died defending their marriage in [[The Scandal of 1776]]. The name was deliberate and defiant, establishing [[The Baudin Tradition]] that would continue for nine generations and counting.

## Marriage to House Northmere

Baudin I married Cereline of [[House Northmere]] (~1800), the first bride from the northern nobility to join House Wilson. This match helped legitimize the exiled house among their new neighbors.

## Children

- Baudin Wilson II (b. ~1802) — heir, continuing the tradition
- Niveline (b. ~1805) — daughter, married Beric Northmere
- Cerald Wilson (b. ~1808) — son, named for his mother

## Legacy

Baudin I was the bridge between exile and establishment. Born in the shadow of scandal, he lived to see House Wilson become an accepted part of the northern nobility.

title: Colardine Wilson
subtitle: First Wilson Daughter — Named for the Kinslayer
content:
**Colardine Wilson** (~1780-~1845) was the second child of [[Lennis Wilfrey]] and [[Nivette Wilfson]], and the first Wilson daughter to marry.

## The Controversial Name

Colardine was named as a feminine form honoring [[Colard Wilfson]] — the brother who killed [[Baudin Wilfson]]. This seemed an odd choice for the child of exiles, but [[Lennis Wilfrey]] reportedly said: "Colard did what he believed was right. We do not hate him for it."

This generosity of spirit — naming a child for the man who killed your wife's brother — says much about the founders' character. They chose forgiveness over bitterness.

## Marriage to House Ashford

Colardine married Rodric Ashford (~1798), becoming the first Wilson daughter to wed. [[House Ashford]]'s acceptance of this match was significant — it signaled that the northern nobility was willing to embrace the exiled family.

## See Also

title: Bauerholt
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfbauer
content:
**Bauerholt** is the seat of [[House Wilfbauer]], located in the western woods of the [[Bramblehall]] region where the forest thins enough for modest farming.

## Setting

Unlike the deep-forest seats, Bauerholt has some open land — enough for grain and livestock. The hall itself is timber-framed, sprawling rather than tall, surrounded by workshops and granaries. Of the three cadet seats, Bauerholt feels the most like a village.

## Character

The Wilfbauers are the most outward-looking of the three woodland branches, their farming bringing them into regular contact with traders and merchants. Where [[Bolewood]] is hidden and [[Barkhollow]] is invisible, Bauerholt welcomes visitors — or at least tolerates them.

## The Woodland Marriage Tradition

Bauerholt has provided brides for Bramblehall's lords as part of the broader [[Woodland Marriage Tradition]]:
- Woodline Wilfbauer → Bors Wilfrey (~1948)

title: Bolewood
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfbole
content:
**Bolewood** is the seat of [[House Wilfbole]], built among ancient oaks so vast that some of the lower chambers are carved into living trunks.

## Setting

The Wilfboles are woodcrafters — carpenters, coopers, bowyers — and their seat reflects their trade. Every beam is hand-selected, every joint mortised with the precision of generations of practice. The oaks here are immense, and the Wilfboles claim some predate the founding of [[House Wilfrey]] itself.

## Character

Of the three cadet branches, the Wilfboles are the most traditional. They keep the old forest rites that even [[Bramblehall]] has half-forgotten. Their knowledge of timber and woodcraft is renowned across the region.

## The Woodland Marriage Tradition

Bolewood has provided brides for Bramblehall's lords as part of the broader [[Woodland Marriage Tradition]]:
- Beraline Wilfbole → Alec Wilfrey (~1975)

title: Barkhollow
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfbark
content:
**Barkhollow** is the seat of [[House Wilfbark]], occupying a natural depression in the deep forest where three streams converge.

## Setting

Half-underground, half-timbered, the seat is nearly invisible from more than a hundred paces — a characteristic the Wilfbarks cultivate deliberately. Approaching Barkhollow without a guide is nearly impossible; the Wilfbarks prefer it that way.

## Character

The Wilfbarks are the hunters, trackers, and wardens of the deep wood. Of the three cadet branches, they are the most insular — which is saying something among [[Bramblehall]]'s already insular people. They know every path, every clearing, every animal run in the forest. Their knowledge of the wood is Bramblehall's greatest strategic asset.

## The Woodland Marriage Tradition

Barkhollow has provided brides for Bramblehall's lords as part of the broader [[Woodland Marriage Tradition]]:
- Mirette Wilfbark → Aldwin Wilfrey (~1825) — the first woodland bride to marry a lord's heir
- Branelisse Wilfbark → Aldric Wilfrey II (~1918)

Borsham Wilfrey (Lord Alec's brother) also married Griseline Wilfbark (~1978).

title: The Woodland Marriage Tradition
subtitle: Bramblehall's Custom of Marrying Within the Forest
content:
**The Woodland Marriage Tradition** is the long-standing custom among the people of [[Bramblehall]] of marrying within the three woodland cadet branches: [[House Wilfbauer]], [[House Wilfbole]], and [[House Wilfbark]].

## The Tradition

Among the broader Bramblehall population — common folk, minor knights, cadet branch members — marrying within the woodland is the norm rather than the exception. The forest is vast, the communities close-knit, and the outside world far away. For most Bramblehall people, a spouse from another woodland family is the natural and expected choice.

## The Heir's Exception

For the lord's heir, however, the expectation has traditionally been different. An heir is expected to marry politically — to strengthen alliances with the other Wilfrey seats or with sworn houses. When a lord's heir DOES marry woodland, it is noteworthy and unusual, even at Bramblehall.

In nine generations of Bramblehall lords, only four have married woodland brides:
- **Aldwin** (Gen 3, ~1825) — married Mirette Wilfbark, the first heir to break convention
- **Aldric II** (Gen 6, ~1918) — married Branelisse Wilfbark
- **Bors** (Gen 7, ~1948) — married Woodline Wilfbauer
- **Alec** (Gen 8, ~1975) — married Beraline Wilfbole

The clustering of three consecutive woodland marriages in the modern era (Aldric II, Bors, Alec) is unprecedented and a source of quiet comment among the other seats.

## Advantages

- Deep loyalty from the woodland cadet branches
- Preservation of old traditions and forest knowledge
- Strong internal cohesion — the Bramblehall people are more closely related than those of any other seat

## Concerns

- Limited genetic diversity among the lordly line (when woodland marriages occur)
- Political isolation from the other Wilfrey seats
- Bramblehall is less connected to the wider Wilfrey network than [[Breakmount Castle|Breakmount]], [[Fourhearth Castle|Fourhearth]], or [[House Wilfrey of Riverhead|Riverhead]]

## The Broader Pattern

While the lord's marriage choice attracts attention, the true strength of the tradition lies in the hundreds of marriages among the common folk, cadet branch members, and minor knights of the Bramblehall woodlands. These marriages — unremarked upon and unremarkable — are the fabric of Bramblehall's insular character.

## See Also
- [[Bramblehall]]: The seat at the centre of the tradition
- [[House Wilfbauer]]: The farming branch (seat: [[Bauerholt]])
- [[House Wilfbole]]: The woodcraft branch (seat: [[Bolewood]])
- [[House Wilfbark]]: The hunting branch (seat: [[Barkhollow]])

title: The Legend of the Ten Daughters
subtitle: How Six Became Ten
content:
**The Legend of the Ten Daughters** refers to the widely-held belief that Lord [[Constann Wilfrey]] of [[Bramblehall]] fathered ten daughters of extraordinary beauty. In truth, Constann had six daughters — Constance, Floriselle, Belisent, Adelise, [[Raylegh]], and [[Giseline Wilfson|Giseline]] — along with two sons.

## The Inflation

The daughters of Bramblehall travelled with retainers and companions, many of them beautiful women in their own right. In the retelling, over generations, the serving women became daughters, the companions became sisters, and six became ten. Stories change. Details shift over the years.

## The Truth

Constann and his wife Florine (of [[House Wilfrey of Riverhead|Riverhead]]) had eight children total, including two sets of boy-girl twins:
- Aldric + Constance (twins, ~1743)
- Floriselle (~1747)
- Borsward + Belisent (twins, ~1749)
- Adelise (~1753)
- Raylegh (~1755)
- Giseline (1758)

## Why It Persists

The Bramblehall people see no reason to correct the legend. Ten daughters sounds grander than six, and the truth — that serving women were confused with highborn ladies — reflects well on Bramblehall's egalitarian character. In the forest, they might say, beauty does not care for rank.

## The Marriages

The six daughters' marriages created a diplomatic web binding Bramblehall to the wider Wilfrey world:
- Constance → [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount]]
- Floriselle → [[House Wilfrey of Fourhearth]]
- Belisent → [[House Hendry]]
- Adelise → [[House Vespen]]
- Raylegh → [[The Old Knight]] (died in childbirth ~1778)
- Giseline → [[House Wilfson]] (married Colard, post-scandal reconciliation)

## See Also
- [[Constann Wilfrey]]: Their father
- [[Bramblehall]]: Where the legend originated
- [[The Scandal of 1776]]: Triggered by daughter Raylegh

title: Constann Wilfrey
subtitle: Lord of Bramblehall — Father of the 'Ten Daughters'
content:
**Constann Wilfrey** (~1725-~1790) was Lord of [[Bramblehall]] during [[The Scandal of 1776]]. He is best known as the father of the legendary 'ten daughters,' though in truth he fathered six daughters and two sons.

## The 'Ten' Daughters

While Lord Constann's daughters became legendary for their beauty, the famed 'ten daughters' is an inflation of history. In truth, Constann fathered six daughters — Constance, Floriselle, Belisent, Adelise, [[Raylegh]], and [[Giseline Wilfson|Giseline]] — along with two sons, Aldric (the heir) and Borsward. The sons came as twins alongside their sisters: Aldric with Constance, Borsward with Belisent.

The legend of ten arose because the daughters travelled with beautiful retainers and companions. Over generations of retelling, the serving women became daughters, the companions became sisters, and six became ten. The Bramblehall people see no reason to correct the story.

The daughters' marriages:
- Constance → [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount]]
- Floriselle → [[House Wilfrey of Fourhearth]]
- Belisent → [[House Hendry]]
- Adelise → [[House Vespen]]
- Raylegh → married [[The Old Knight]]; died in childbirth ~1778
- Giseline → [[House Wilfson]] (Colard, post-scandal reconciliation)

## After the Scandal

Constann lived another 14 years after the scandal (~1776-1790). He watched his daughter Giseline marry the kinslayer [[Colard Wilfson]] in 1778 — a gesture of reconciliation from Bramblehall, forgiving the chaos that originated from their seat. He honoured the original betrothal of Raylegh to [[The Old Knight]], and when she died in childbirth shortly after, he never spoke publicly of it. Whether his silence was grief, guilt, or dignity, no one can say.

## See Also

- [[Raylegh]]: His daughter who triggered the scandal
- [[The Legend of the Ten Daughters]]: The myth that grew from his family

title: House Wilfmarsh
subtitle: Cadet Branch of Riverhead
content:
**House Wilfmarsh** is a cadet branch of [[House Wilfrey of Riverhead]], seated at [[Fenholm]] in the marshy lowlands where the river broadens into wetlands.

## Origin

Founded by a younger son of the Riverhead line who was granted the fens — land no one else wanted. Where [[House Wilfriver]] took the profitable river trade, the Wilfmarsh branch received the bogs. They made the best of it.

## Character

The Wilfmarsh family manages drainage, flood control, and the eel-catching that feeds much of Riverhead's lower population. They are practical, unglamorous, and reliable. Their reputation is the inverse of the Wilfrivers: where Wilfriver has moderate standing and ill repute (smuggling suspicions, sharp dealing), Wilfmarsh has low standing but good repute. They are trusted precisely because they have nothing worth stealing.

## Economy

- **Eel-catching**: The fens produce vast quantities of eels — smoked, salted, and traded upriver
- **Drainage**: Wilfmarsh engineers maintain the dikes and channels that keep the lowlands habitable
- **Flood management**: When the river swells, it is the Wilfmarsh who open and close the sluices
- **Peat**: Cut from the bogs for fuel, traded locally

## Relations

The Wilfmarsh are loyal to Riverhead but have little contact with the other Wilfrey seats. Their world is the fen — its rhythms, its floods, its eels. They attend Wilfrey councils when summoned but contribute little to political maneuvering. Their value is in their work, not their words.

## Current Head

[[Godwin Wilfmarsh]] (b. 1950) is master of Fenholm. His heir is [[Harwin Wilfmarsh]].

## See Also
- [[House Wilfrey of Riverhead]]: The parent seat
- [[House Wilfriver]]: The other Riverhead cadet — contrasting reputation
- [[Fenholm]]: The Wilfmarsh seat

title: Banehold
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfsbane
content:
**Banehold** is the seat of [[House Wilfsbane]], a cadet branch of [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount]]. It guards the high passes above the silver mines of [[Night Mountain]].

## Location

Perched on a ridge above the treeline, Banehold commands the mountain passes that connect the Breakmount silver mines to the lowland trade routes. The position is harsh — cold winds, thin soil, and long winters — but strategically vital. No ore leaves [[Night Mountain]] without passing under Wilfsbane eyes.

## Architecture

Banehold is more fortress than hall. Built from the same dark stone as the mountain itself, it hunches against the wind like a clenched fist. There is no great hall for feasting — the Wilfsbane eat in a vaulted guardroom. Comfort was never the point.

## Economy

The Wilfsbane do not mine the silver themselves — that is Breakmount's domain. They guard the passes and levy tolls on the ore convoys, taking a fixed share as their right. In lean years, this makes them richer than their masters; in boom years, merely comfortable.

## See Also
- [[House Wilfsbane]]: The house seated here
- [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount]]: The parent seat
- [[Night Mountain]]: The silver mines below

title: Fourgate
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfour
content:
**Fourgate** is the seat of [[House Wilfour]], a cadet branch of [[House Wilfrey of Fourhearth]]. It controls the harbour entrance at [[Fourhearth Castle]].

## Location

Fourgate sits at the mouth of Fourhearth's harbour, built on the promontory that forms the eastern breakwater. Every vessel entering or leaving the harbour passes under its walls. The position is profoundly commercial — less about defence than about taxation.

## Architecture

A handsome stone tower with attached warehouses and a customs hall. Unlike the grim fortresses of the mountain cadets, Fourgate is designed to impress merchants and intimidate smugglers in equal measure. The Wilfour arms fly above the harbour chain.

## Economy

The Wilfour collect harbour dues on behalf of Fourhearth, retaining a share. They also maintain pilot boats that guide vessels through the harbour entrance — a service that is technically optional but practically mandatory, as captains who refuse the pilot tend to find the channel markers moved.

This makes House Wilfour the wealthiest of all the cadet branches across every Wilfrey seat.

## See Also

title: Sandholme
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfsands
content:
**Sandholme** is the seat of [[House Wilfsands]], a cadet branch of [[House Wilfrey of Fourhearth]]. It sits on the tidal flats south of the harbour.

## Location

Built on a raised platform above the high-tide line, Sandholme overlooks a vast expanse of sandbanks, mudflats, and shallow channels. At low tide the flats stretch for miles; at high tide the sea comes almost to the walls. The Wilfsands know every current and quicksand, every safe crossing and every death-trap.

## Architecture

Sandholme is built low and wide — a single-storey compound of salt-bleached stone with deep foundations driven into the sand. It floods once or twice a generation during exceptional tides, and the Wilfsands accept this with the fatalism of people who live at the mercy of the sea.

## Economy

- **Salt-panning**: Shallow pools along the flats evaporate seawater for salt — a steady trade
- **Shellfish**: Oysters, mussels, and cockles from the tidal beds
- **Salvage rights**: Wrecked vessels on the sandbanks belong to House Wilfsands by ancient custom

Less wealthy than the Wilfours but more self-sufficient. The Wilfsands could survive a siege indefinitely — the sea feeds them.

## See Also
- [[House Wilfsands]]: The house seated here
- [[House Wilfrey of Fourhearth]]: The parent seat
- [[House Wilfour]]: The other Fourhearth cadet — wealthier but more dependent on trade

title: Fenholm
subtitle: Seat of House Wilfmarsh
content:
**Fenholm** is the seat of [[House Wilfmarsh]], a cadet branch of [[House Wilfrey of Riverhead]]. It sits in the marshy lowlands where the river broadens into wetlands.

## Location

Fenholm occupies a low island — barely above the waterline — in the middle of the fen. Access is by causeway or punt. In wet seasons the causeway floods and the only way in or out is by boat. This isolation is both the house's weakness and its defence: no army has ever besieged Fenholm, because no army could find it.

## Architecture

Built of timber and wattle on oak pilings driven into the marsh. Fenholm is not a castle in any conventional sense — more a collection of connected buildings rising out of the reeds. The main hall is thatched, the kitchens smoke-blackened, and the whole place smells of peat and eels. Visitors from the stone castles of Breakmount or Fourhearth find it primitive. The Wilfmarsh find it home.

## Economy

The fens provide:
- **Eels**: The primary export — smoked, salted, and traded upriver
- **Wildfowl**: Duck, heron, and other marsh birds
- **Peat**: Cut and dried for fuel
- **Rush and reed**: For thatching and basket-weaving

None of these make the Wilfmarsh wealthy. All of them make the Wilfmarsh self-sufficient.

title: Bastard Naming Conventions
subtitle: The Dun- and Dum- Prefix System
content:
**Bastard Naming Conventions** are the system by which illegitimate children are identified in the wider world. The two prefixes — **Dun** and **Dum** — indicate which parent's noble name the bastard carries.

## Dun- Prefix (Father's Name)

The far more common form. A bastard acknowledged by a noble father takes the prefix "Dun-" before the father's house name. For example:
- **Dunwilfrey**: bastard of a Wilfrey lord
- **Dunwilfson**: bastard of a Wilfson man
- **Dunwilfern**: bastard of a Wilfern knight
- **Dunwilfriver**: bastard of a Wilfriver man
- **Dunwilson**: bastard of a Wilson lord

Dun-named bastards are typically acknowledged, often raised near the family (though rarely within it), and sometimes serve the house as men-at-arms, servants, or labourers. They carry enough of the name to open some doors and close others.

## Dum- Prefix (Mother's Name)

Far rarer — roughly one bastard in eight bears the mother's name rather than the father's. A child takes the Dum- prefix when:
1. The father is unknown, common, or refuses acknowledgement
2. The mother's noble name carries more weight than the father's
3. The mother (or her family) insists on it

For example:
- **Dumwilfrey**: bastard of a Wilfrey woman — the Wilfrey name is valuable enough that some mothers choose it deliberately
- **Dumwilfriver**: bastard of a Wilfriver woman

Dum-named bastards are placed in the Commoner class more often than Dun-named ones, as their fathers typically have no house to claim them.

## The Wilfrey Exception

In most families, the Dum- prefix is exceedingly rare. But in the Wilfrey context, the mother's name carries unusual weight. A Dumwilfrey is still a Wilfrey — even a bastard Wilfrey is a name worth having. This makes Dum-named bastards slightly more common among Wilfrey women than in other houses, though still well below the Dun- rate.

## Social Standing

Bastards occupy a liminal space: not noble, not common, but caught between. A Dunwilfrey in the harbour towns of [[Fourhearth Castle]] might be respected for the name; in the halls of [[Breakmount Castle]], the same name marks them as an embarrassment. Context is everything.

## See Also
- [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount]]: Has the most recorded Dunwilfrey bastards
- [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall]]: Woodland culture kept bastards quieter until recently
- [[House Wilfrey of Fourhearth]]: Home to both Dunwilfrey and Dumwilfrey bastards

title: Wyrmwood Forest
subtitle: The Great Forest of the Southern Wilfrey Lands
content:
**Wyrmwood Forest** (colloquially 'the Wyrmwood') is the great forest lying along the southern border of [[House Wilfrey]]'s lands, encompassing the territories granted to [[Bram Wilfrey]] in 1176. [[Bramblehall]] stands at its edge.

## Geography

The Wyrmwood is vast and ancient, forming a natural boundary along the southern reaches of Wilfrey territory. Its interior is dense, layered, and largely impenetrable to those without knowledge of its ways. The forest contains several notable sites: [[Haligdene]], [[Greenweft]], [[Thornweald]], and [[Mosshollow]] — sacred gardens tended by the forest-folk on behalf of [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall]].

## The Forest-Folk

Wyrmwood has been inhabited since before the Wilfreys' arrival. When [[Bram Wilfrey]] received his grant from the [[Crown of Estargenn]] in 1176, he found the forest already managed by communities of forest-dwellers who understood its rhythms and resources. Rather than displace them, he formalized the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]] — a compact that binds the forest-folk to Bramblehall's service while preserving their autonomy and way of life.

The forest-folk maintain a pattern of **seasonal circulation** — semi-nomadic movement through the forest following the rhythms of growth and harvest, managing natural regeneration through controlled movement rather than permanent settlement.

## Thirren

The Wyrmwood's most strategically valuable resource is [[Thirren]] (known in trade as Greyfast, to soldiers as Shieldwood) — a timber that grows only here under proper cultivation. The forest-folk's irreplaceable expertise in managing thirren groves forms the economic foundation of the entire relationship between forest and hall.

## The Wytherns

Among the forest-folk, the [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] family holds a position of unspoken prominence — the oldest family, tenders of [[Haligdene]], keepers of the deepest traditions. They are not nobles in any formal sense, but carry the quiet authority of people who have been doing the same thing, in the same place, longer than anyone can remember.

## Chain of Allegiance

Forest-folk → [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]] → [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount|Breakmount]] → [[Crown of Estargenn|Crown]]

**See Also:** [[Bramblehall]] · [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]] · [[Thirren]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[Bram Wilfrey]]

title: Bram Wilfrey
subtitle: First Lord of Bramblehall
content:
**Bram Wilfrey** (born 1155) was the second son of the [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount|Breakmount Wilfreys]] and the founder of [[Bramblehall]] in 1176.

## The Grant

During a significant conflict, Bram performed feats of extraordinary bravery that shifted a crucial battle and turned the tide of the entire conflict in the [[Crown of Estargenn|Crown]]'s favour. For this service beyond service, the Crown granted him all the forest lands of [[Wyrmwood Forest]] and many other territories besides.

He was made [[Drithen]] — equal to many Great Drithen whose families had long-established histories and storied pasts — answerable only to his own Drihten at [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount|Breakmount]] and to the Crown itself.

No one ever held the grant against him. No one had ever earned it so magnificently.

## The Wood-Warden's Oath

When Bram came to Wyrmwood Forest, he found it already inhabited and already managed — not by lords, but by folk who knew the forest's ways. The forest-dwellers were practiced stewards who had maintained the wood for generations uncounted, managing food reserves, cultivating special flora, and — most crucially — knowing the secrets of [[Thirren]], the valuable timber the forest produced.

Bram, having earned his position through merit, recognised merit in others. Rather than displace the forest-folk or impose traditional vassalage, he formalized the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]] — an arrangement that acknowledged the forest-folk's expertise and autonomy while binding them to Bramblehall's protection and purpose.

It was a partnership born of mutual recognition, not conquest.

**See Also:** [[Bramblehall]] · [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]] · [[Thirren]] · [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount]]

title: Thirren
subtitle: The Strategic Timber of Wyrmwood Forest
content:
**Thirren** is a strategic timber that grows only in [[Wyrmwood Forest]] under proper cultivation. It is known by several names across [[Estargenn]]:

- **Greyfast** — the trade name
- **Shieldwood** — the soldiers' term
- **Lignum Tenax** — the scholarly designation

## Properties

- Lighter than oak with equal strength
- Resists shattering in combat better than traditional shield woods
- Strong, workable, and weather-resistant for construction
- Produces valuable sap used in medicines, adhesives, and preservatives
- Grows only in Wyrmwood under proper cultivation

## Worked Thirren

Beyond its military and construction uses, thirren's fine grain and exceptional longevity make it prized for decorative and personal items. Greyfast beaded necklaces, carved ear stretchers, and settings for fine jewels are sought after for their beauty and remarkable durability — thirren-work outlasts the wearer by generations, becoming heirloom pieces passed down through families. The warm grey tone of worked thirren deepens with age rather than degrading, making old pieces more beautiful than new.

## Forest-Folk Expertise

The forest-folk of Wyrmwood possess irreplaceable knowledge of thirren cultivation:
- Which groves to harvest and which to leave fallow
- Seasonal rhythms of growth
- Techniques for encouraging straight grain and dense wood
- Secrets of sap extraction and processing
- Regeneration management for sustainable harvest

This expertise cannot be replicated by outsiders. Any lord could claim a forest; few could make it produce what the forest-folk can coax from Wyrmwood.

## Economic Importance

Thirren forms the economic foundation of the entire [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]]. [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]] profits enormously from thirren trade, but the resource exists only because of forest-folk stewardship. This mutual dependence — Bramblehall cannot replicate the knowledge, forest-folk cannot market without Bramblehall's protection — is the pragmatic heart of the Compact.

**See Also:** [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]] · [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall]] · [[The Wytherns]]

title: The Wytherns
subtitle: Ancient Forest-Folk of Wyrmwood
content:
**The Wytherns** are the oldest known family among the forest-folk of [[Wyrmwood Forest]]. They claim descent from the legendary [[Harfalene Greenfinger]], a figure who predates the Wilfreys' arrival. They have never been nobles, never attempted nobility, and never held a seat in any formal hierarchy.

Yet among the forest-folk, the Wytherns carry an authority that needs no title. It is not the authority of lords — not rank within the structures of [[Driht]] and fealty that govern [[Estargenn]]'s noble houses. It is something older and quieter: a mystical leadership capacity, recognised by their forest-folk peers but never discussed, only felt. When a Wythern speaks at the [[Seasonal Gatherings|seasonal gatherings]], others listen — not because they must, but because something in the listening feels right. They are de facto leaders, though this is never stated, only implied, and never enforced.

This soft authority arises from the consistency of their way of life — the same gardens tended, the same stories told, the same slow rhythms observed for centuries while the world beyond the treeline changes and forgets. The Wytherns are the forest-folk who stayed truest to the oldest ways. That faithfulness is their credential.

## Way of Life

The Wytherns follow the ancient pattern of **seasonal circulation** through Wyrmwood's depths — semi-nomadic movement following the rhythms of growth and harvest. Their great work is the stewarding of the forest's sacred gardens on behalf of [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]]:

- [[Haligdene]] — the moon-garden, most sacred of all Wyrmwood sites
- [[Greenweft]] — medicinal herbs and gathering grounds
- [[Thornweald]] — ancient orchards of half-wild fruit
- [[Mosshollow]] — fungal gardens and preservation beds

They also manage [[Thirren]] groves, holding traditional knowledge of which stands to harvest and which to protect.

## The Oath

The Wytherns are sworn to Bramblehall through the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]], as are all forest-folk. But they also keep the older [[The Stewardship Oath|Stewardship Oath]] — a personal commitment to tend [[Haligdene]] that predates any noble arrangement.

## Relations with Other Forest-Folk

The Wytherns' unspoken prominence is a source of both unity and tension. Other families — notably [[Corven Ashwood]] and his kin — resent the quiet assumption that Wytherns lead the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter delegation]] and present the [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]] to the Lord of Bramblehall. These families cultivate [[Thirren]] just as expertly and serve the Compact just as faithfully, yet lack the Wytherns' aura of ancient belonging.

The tension is real but rarely erupts. It is the politics of respect, not power.

## Connection to House Wilfrey

The Wytherns hold no Wilfrey blood and claim no kinship. From Bramblehall's perspective, they are commoners — but commoners the Wilfreys treat differently, sensing an unnameable weight in Wythern voices. This is not privilege of birth but gravity of presence. The Wilfreys regard the Wytherns with a mixture of respect and incomprehension: folk who chose the forest over everything else the world could offer, and who seem richer for it.

## Current Wytherns

- [[Eldric Wythern]] — Eldest Steward of Haligdene
- [[Maris Wythern]] — Keeper of Greenweft
- [[Theren Wythern]] — Young steward, Eldric's grandson

**See Also:** [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]] · [[Haligdene]] · [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] · [[Corven Ashwood]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]]

title: The Wood-Warden's Oath
subtitle: The Compact Between Forest and Hall
content:
**The Wood-Warden's Oath** (also called the **Warden's Compact** or the **Green Covenant**) is the arrangement binding the forest-folk of [[Wyrmwood Forest]] to [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall]]. It was formalized by [[Bram Wilfrey]] in 1176 when he took lordship, though built upon older patterns of forest stewardship that preceded any noble claim.

## What the Forest-Folk Owe

- **Stewardship of the wood** — managing Wyrmwood's health and abundance through seasonal circulation
- **Cultivation of [[Thirren]]** — growing, managing, and harvesting the strategic timber
- **Management of forest resources** — tending food reserves, special flora, medicinal plants
- **Right of passage** — safe conduct for Wilfrey parties; guidance when requested
- **Wood-knowledge** — counsel on forest matters; warning of threats
- **[[The Midwinter Tribute|Tribute of Plenty]]** — annual offering presented at Bramblehall on Midwinter's Day
- **[[The Mustering-Right]]** — answering the call to arms in defence of the realm, invoked sparingly

## What the Forest-Folk Do Not Owe

- Regular military service or standing levies
- Attendance at court or council
- Taxes in coin or crops beyond the Midwinter Tribute
- Submission to Bramblehall's justice in internal forest matters (they govern themselves)
- Participation in political disputes between noble houses

## What House Wilfrey Owes in Return

- **Protection of forest-rights** — no timber cutting, hunting, or settlement without consultation
- **Defence against outsiders** — Bramblehall's strength shields the forest-folk
- **Non-interference** — forest-folk govern themselves; Bramblehall does not impose laws or judges
- **Sacred recognition** — acknowledgment of the forest-folk's ancient relationship with the land
- **Fair trade in [[Thirren]]** — forest-folk receive portion of trade proceeds

## Renewal

The Compact is renewed ceremonially every generation when a new Lord or Lady of Bramblehall takes their seat.

## Economic Foundation

The Compact is not merely tradition or kindness — it is economically rational. Bramblehall could theoretically impose traditional vassalage, but doing so would likely destroy the forest-folk's willingness and ability to manage thirren properly. The forest-folk could theoretically withhold their expertise, but doing so would invite retaliation and loss of protection. The relationship works because both parties genuinely need each other.

## Chain of Allegiance

Forest-folk → [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]] → [[House Wilfrey of Breakmount|Breakmount]] → [[Crown of Estargenn|Crown]]

Forest-folk have no direct oath to Breakmount, but ultimate obligations flow upward through proper channels.

**See Also:** [[Bram Wilfrey]] · [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[Thirren]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]] · [[The Mustering-Right]] · [[The Wytherns]]

title: Haligdene
subtitle: The Holy Vale of Wyrmwood
content:
**Haligdene** (Holy Vale) is a sacred valley deep within [[Wyrmwood Forest]] — the most hallowed site of [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] culture and possibly of pre-Wilfrey forest-folk tradition.

## The Valley

Haligdene is a place of extraordinary natural abundance. Whether by some quality of the soil, the water, or something less easily named, things grow here with a fecundity unmatched elsewhere in the Wyrmwood. The valley is said to be accessible only to those it 'chooses' — an assertion that may reflect spiritual truth, practical enforcement by the Wytherns, or simply the difficulty of navigating the deep forest without guidance.

## The Mirellune Beds

Haligdene is home to the [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]] — Moon's Mercy, the Pale Flower — which blooms only beneath moonrise. The first recorded cultivation of Mirellune beds is attributed to [[Harfalene Wythern]] in the early 13th century, though the legendary [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] is said to have known the valley centuries before.

All five sacred flowers of the Wythern tradition grow here: Mirellune, Thistrelace, Aelwynne, Eiribel, and Halithrae.

## Stewardship

Those who would tend Haligdene must swear the [[The Stewardship Oath|Stewardship Oath]] — an ancient commitment spoken at the moment of first moonrise in the valley, in the presence of blooming Mirellune, witnessed by at least three elder stewards.

## The Mirellune Taboo

*Those who take more than one are said never to find the valley again.*

Each year, a single stem is cut at moonrise by the eldest living Wythern who has kept the Stewardship Oath and presented at the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter Tribute]] to the Lord or Lady of [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]]. This is the only Mirellune that ever leaves the valley.

**See Also:** [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene]] · [[The Stewardship Oath]] · [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] · [[Harfalene Wythern]]

title: Greenweft
subtitle: Healing Grounds of Wyrmwood
content:
**Greenweft** is one of the famous gardens of [[Wyrmwood Forest]], tended by the forest-folk on behalf of [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]]. It is known for its medicinal herbs and healing grounds, serving as an informal infirmary for the forest-folk.

## Gathering Site

Greenweft serves as the principal meeting place for the [[Seasonal Gatherings|quarterly seasonal gatherings]] where forest-folk assemble for knowledge-sharing, dispute resolution, and arrangement of marriages. Three days before [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter]], Greenweft hosts the largest gathering of the year — when the delegation is chosen, tribute goods assembled, [[Thirren]] harvest assessed, and grievances discussed.

## Current Keeper

[[Maris Wythern]], skilled herbalist and healer, currently maintains Greenweft.

**See Also:** [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[Maris Wythern]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]] · [[Seasonal Gatherings]]

title: The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene
subtitle: The Five Flowers of the Holy Vale
content:
Five sacred flowers grow in [[Haligdene]], each tended with ritualistic care by the [[The Wytherns|Wytherns]] and harvested only according to proper season and rite. Each flower is also used in the [[The Flower-Naming Tradition|Flower-Naming]] tradition.

## Mirellune
*Moon's Mercy / The Pale Flower*

The most sacred flower of Haligdene. Blooms only beneath moonrise. Central to Wythern identity and the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter Tribute]] — each year a single stem is cut by the eldest steward and presented to the Lord or Lady of [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]]. The flower is said to bloom throughout the twelve days of Midwinter if the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Compact]] holds true, but to wither within hours if either party has broken faith. In living memory, the flower has never withered.

*Those who take more than one are said never to find the valley again.*

Rarely given as a flower-name — only to children born beneath a full moon within sight of Haligdene.

## Thistrelace
*The Woven Flower / Wind's Gift*

Appears as a weaving of thistle and lace without fully belonging to either. Petals said to move like cloth in a breeze. Children swear it hums when the valley is quiet. Given as a flower-name to girls thought fey-touched or born during windstorms.

## Aelwynne
*Dawn's Breath / The Halig Bloom*

Said to glow faintly at dawn and dusk. Some believe speaking its name aloud draws its petals closed. Given as a flower-name to children born at liminal hours — dawn or dusk.

## Eiribel
*The Silent Bell / Rain-Caller*

Its name sounds like a bell when spoken. Believed to ring soundlessly when touched by rain. Gathered only after storms — otherwise cannot be found. Given as a flower-name to children born during storms or who first cry at the sound of rain.

## Halithrae
*Veilpetal / The Thin Bloom*

Name derived from 'Halig' (holy). Believed to mark places where the veil between worlds grows thin. One cannot seek it, only notice it. Given as a flower-name to children who seem to walk between worlds — often sickly or unusually perceptive.

**See Also:** [[Haligdene]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Flower-Naming Tradition]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]]

title: The Midwinter Tribute
subtitle: Annual Ceremony of the Warden's Compact
content:
**The Midwinter Tribute** (also called the **Tribute of Plenty**) is the annual ceremony on the longest night when representatives of the forest-folk of [[Wyrmwood Forest]] present tribute goods to the Lord or Lady of [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]] — not as tax, but as demonstration of the forest's abundance and the forest-folk's faithful stewardship.

## The Ceremony

1. **The Gathering at Greenweft** — Forest-folk assemble at [[Greenweft]] three days before Midwinter to select representatives, assemble tribute goods, assess the year's [[Thirren]] harvest, and discuss any grievances
2. **The Journey to Bramblehall** — A delegation travels to the hall, traditionally led by a Wythern elder (by custom, not by rule)
3. **The Presentation** — Goods are laid before the Lord or Lady:
   - Herbs from [[Greenweft]]
   - Fruits from [[Thornweald]]
   - Preserved foods from [[Mosshollow]]
   - Sample timbers of [[Thirren]], demonstrating the year's harvest quality
   - A single stem of [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]] from [[Haligdene]]
4. **The Renewal** — The Lord or Lady speaks the words of the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Warden's Compact]]; the forest representative responds with the ancient acceptance
5. **The Feast** — Forest-folk are hosted at Bramblehall for the Midwinter feast, a rare mingling of hall and wood

## The Mirellune Presentation

The single stem of Mirellune is always presented by a [[The Wytherns|Wythern]], and always to the Lord or Lady directly — never to a proxy. This is the moment when the Wytherns' quiet prominence is most visible, and it is a source of resentment among other forest-folk families who serve the Compact just as faithfully.

The Mirellune is said to bloom throughout the twelve days of Midwinter if the Compact holds true, but to wither within hours if either party has broken faith. In living memory, the flower has never withered.

**See Also:** [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]] · [[Bramblehall]] · [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene]]

title: The Mustering-Right
subtitle: Bramblehall's Power to Call the Forest to Arms
content:
**The Mustering-Right** is [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]]'s power to call the forest-folk of [[Wyrmwood Forest]] to arms under the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]].

## Historical Use

The mustering has been invoked only seven times since the Compact was first sworn, always in moments of existential threat to the realm. Forest-folk fight differently than armoured knights — they are scouts, guerrilla fighters, ambushers, masters of terrain. A forest-folk levy is small in number but devastating in their home territory.

## Contemporary Tension

The most contentious element of the Wood-Warden's Oath. Younger forest-folk question whether this obligation still serves:

- [[Theren Wythern]] asks whether forest-folk should die in wars unrelated to the forest, especially when mustering pulls them from crucial [[Thirren]] management during growing seasons
- [[Corven Ashwood]] questions the obligation from a different angle — if the forest-folk fight, they should have more say in the Compact's terms
- [[Eldric Wythern]] represents the traditional view: *The oath is the oath. Without Bramblehall's protection, what prevents timber merchants and settlers from destroying Wyrmwood?*

This tension remains unresolved, simmering beneath the otherwise harmonious relationship between hall and wood.

**See Also:** [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]] · [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall]] · [[Theren Wythern]] · [[Eldric Wythern]]

title: Harfalene Greenfinger
subtitle: Legendary Founder of the Wythern Tradition
content:
**Harfalene Greenfinger** is the legendary founder figure of the [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] tradition — a figure said to have lived in [[Wyrmwood Forest]] before the Wilfreys ever came to these lands.

## The Tale

The story, passed from hearth to hearth in the half-sung cadence of forest folk, speaks of a youth of uncommon grace who walked into [[Haligdene]] and was forever changed. Deep within that hallowed valley he met a woman of the woods — [[The Faire of Haligdene|a faire]] whose beauty put even the Pale Flower to shame. Devoted to the valley itself, he tended the flower beds, learning the ways of root and leaf, until Haligdene became a place of such abundance that folk said the valley had taken him as husband.

His hands, which had known no labour before, became so skilled that all called him **Greenfinger**. When he passed from this world, the valley folk remembered him as **Wythern** — one who belongs to the wood. And his children, and their children after, carried that name into the centuries.

## Legend and History

Whether Harfalene Greenfinger truly existed is impossible to determine. The story predates the Wilfreys' arrival (pre-1176), and no written record confirms or denies it. Centuries later, [[Harfalene Wythern]] — a historical figure — seemed to fulfill the legendary pattern, merging myth and history into a single narrative.

The Wytherns see no contradiction in this. The story is told, not written, and each telling is true in its own way.

title: Harfalene Wythern
subtitle: Historical Founder of the Haligdene Stewardship
content:
**Harfalene Wythern** (fl. early 13th century) is the historical figure most closely associated with the founding of the [[Haligdene]] stewardship tradition.

## Life

A forest-folk man with an uncommon gift for growing things, Harfalene ventured deep into [[Wyrmwood Forest]] seeking land where he might make a life of his own measure. What he found was the valley that would become known as Haligdene — a place of such natural fecundity that he recognised it at once as sacred ground.

There he settled. There he cultivated the first recorded [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]] beds, coaxing that moon-blessed flower from wild scatter into ordered beauty. And there he took to wife a woman of the forest-folk — unlettered, unnamed in the [[Bramblehall]] records, but practical and strong.

## Greenfinger

In tending Haligdene with such skill, people began to call him **Greenfinger** — echoing the ancient tale of [[Harfalene Greenfinger]], the legendary figure who may or may not have walked the same valley centuries before. Whether this was deliberate homage or coincidence, the echo completed a circle. The story and the history merged.

## Legacy

Harfalene Wythern established the patterns that the Wytherns follow to this day: the tending of the Mirellune beds, the slow stewardship of the valley, the understanding that Haligdene reveals itself to whom it will. His descendants multiplied into the loose network of Wythern families who form the spiritual core of [[Wyrmwood Forest]]'s forest-folk community.

**See Also:** [[Haligdene]] · [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Faire of Haligdene]] · [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene]]

title: The Faire of Haligdene
subtitle: Legendary Woman of the Valley
content:
**The Faire of Haligdene** is a figure who exists between legend and history.

In the ancient folklore of [[Wyrmwood Forest]] — the tale of [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] — she is a supernatural woman of the woods, a faire whose beauty put even the Pale Flower to shame. The original Harfalene met her in [[Haligdene]] and was forever changed.

In the historical record of the 13th century, [[Harfalene Wythern]]'s wife was an unnamed woodwoman — practical, strong, unlettered, herself descended from families who had lived in Wyrmwood since before the Wilfreys' arrival.

The two accounts may describe different women centuries apart. They may be the same story told differently. The forest-folk see no need to resolve the question.

**See Also:** [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] · [[Harfalene Wythern]] · [[Haligdene]]

title: Eldric Wythern
subtitle: Eldest Steward of Haligdene
content:
**Eldric Wythern** is the Eldest Steward of [[Haligdene]], having tended the sacred valley for thirty-two years. He is considered the living authority on the valley's lore and proper cultivation methods.

## Role

Eldric has led the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter delegation]] to [[Bramblehall]] for the past fifteen years and personally cuts the [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]] stem for presentation to the Lord of Bramblehall. He is deeply involved in [[Thirren]] management, holding traditional knowledge of which groves to harvest.

## Character

A strong defender of both the [[The Stewardship Oath|Stewardship Oath]] and the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]], Eldric sees them as inseparable commitments. He believes the Compact protects the forest-folk from the encroaching world and must be honoured scrupulously.

His grandson [[Theren Wythern]]'s questioning of the old ways creates tension between them, though their mutual love of Haligdene prevents true rupture.

**See Also:** [[Haligdene]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]] · [[Theren Wythern]]

title: Maris Wythern
subtitle: Keeper of Greenweft
content:
**Maris Wythern** is the Keeper of [[Greenweft]], skilled herbalist and healer who maintains the medicinal gardens of [[Wyrmwood Forest]].

## Role

Maris serves as intermediary between [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] families, other forest-folk, and occasional travellers who seek forest remedies. More open to outsiders than most Wytherns.

## Character

Maris represents the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter Tribute]] delegation pragmatically, arguing for a stronger negotiating position with [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]] — not breaking the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Compact]], but ensuring it evolves to meet contemporary needs. She believes [[Thirren]] management gives the forest-folk economic leverage that should be used wisely.

**See Also:** [[Greenweft]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]]

title: Theren Wythern
subtitle: Young Steward of Haligdene
content:
**Theren Wythern** is a young steward who recently swore the [[The Stewardship Oath|Stewardship Oath]] at [[Haligdene]]. He is the grandson of [[Eldric Wythern]].

## Character

Theren represents the new generation of Wytherns who wonder whether the old isolation can be maintained in changing times. He has expressed interest in establishing more formal trade relationships with [[Bramblehall]] settlements — not as tax or tithe, but as partnership that benefits both forest and hall.

He questions whether the [[The Mustering-Right|Mustering-Right]] still serves forest-folk interests, especially when it pulls them away from crucial [[Thirren]] management during growing seasons.

## The Generational Tension

Theren's views create tension with his grandfather Eldric, though their mutual love of Haligdene prevents true rupture. Where Eldric sees the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Compact]] as sacred and inviolable, Theren sees it as a living arrangement that must adapt or become a cage.

**See Also:** [[Haligdene]] · [[Eldric Wythern]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Mustering-Right]]

title: Corven Ashwood
subtitle: Voice of the Non-Wythern Forest-Folk
content:
**Corven Ashwood** is an influential voice among the non-Wythern forest families of [[Wyrmwood Forest]]. A skilled tracker, hunter, and expert [[Thirren]] cultivator with knowledge equal to any [[The Wytherns|Wythern]].

## Position

Corven maintains that the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]] should be honoured, but argues that [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] soft-leadership of the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter delegation]] perpetuates an unfair hierarchy. He advocates for rotating the [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]] presentation among all forest-folk families, rather than leaving it as a Wythern tradition.

## The Deeper Tension

Corven's challenge is that his grievance is difficult to articulate in concrete terms. The Wytherns hold no title, claim no formal authority, and would deny any special status if asked. Their prominence is a thing of aura and tradition, not rule — and that makes it harder to argue against than any title would be. He can cultivate thirren as well as any Wythern, but he cannot carry their weight of ancient belonging.

He has significant support among younger forest-folk who share his frustration.

**See Also:** [[Wyrmwood Forest]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Midwinter Tribute]] · [[Thirren]]

title: The Stewardship Oath
subtitle: Ancient Oath of Haligdene's Tenders
content:
**The Stewardship Oath** is the ancient commitment sworn by those who would tend [[Haligdene]]. It is separate from and older than the [[The Wood-Warden's Oath|Wood-Warden's Oath]] to [[House Wilfrey of Bramblehall|Bramblehall]].

## The Oath

It must be spoken aloud during the first moonrise in the valley, in the presence of blooming [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene|Mirellune]], witnessed by at least three elder stewards:

*"By root and leaf, by moon and seed,*
*I bind my days to beauty's need,*
*To tend what grows, to guard what gleams,*
*To walk the wood through waking dreams."*

## The Curse

Breaking the Stewardship Oath is said to bring the valley's curse — the oathbreaker will wander [[Wyrmwood Forest|Wyrmwood]] until their death and never find Haligdene again, no matter how well they once knew the way.

## Relationship to the Compact

The [[The Wytherns|Wytherns]] keep both the Stewardship Oath and the Wood-Warden's Oath, seeing them as complementary rather than contradictory. Tending the sacred garden and managing the forest on behalf of a lord are aspects of the same commitment to stewardship.

**See Also:** [[Haligdene]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[The Wood-Warden's Oath]]

title: The Flower-Naming Tradition
subtitle: Wythern Children's Secret Names
content:
**The Flower-Naming Tradition** is the [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] custom of giving children second names drawn from the flora of [[Wyrmwood Forest]]. These names are whispered at birth and spoken only by close kin, serving as a spiritual identity separate from the common name used in daily life.

## The Flower-Names

| Name | Translation | Given To |
|------|------------|----------|
| **Thistrelace** | The Woven Flower | Girls thought fey-touched or born during windstorms |
| **Aelwynne** | Dawn's Breath | Children born at dawn or dusk |
| **Eiribel** | The Silent Bell | Children born during storms or who first cry at rain |
| **Halithrae** | Veilpetal | Sickly or unusually perceptive children |
| **Mirellune** | Moon's Mercy | Rarely given; only for children born beneath a full moon within sight of [[Haligdene]] |

## Significance

The flower-name connects a Wythern child to [[Haligdene]] and to the sacred heritage of the forest. It is not used publicly — to speak another's flower-name without invitation would be a deep transgression. The name belongs to the space between kin, spoken in firelight, whispered in greeting.

**See Also:** [[The Sacred Flowers of Haligdene]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[Haligdene]]

title: The Story-Tradition
subtitle: Oral Lore of the Wytherns
content:
**The Story-Tradition** is the [[The Wytherns|Wythern]] practice of transmitting the tale of [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] — and all their lore — through speech alone. The story is never written, only spoken, passed from elder to youngling in the half-light of evening fires.

## Multiple Versions

Each family maintains its own version of the tale, with particular emphasis on different elements:
- Some stress that Harfalene Greenfinger lived before the Wilfreys came, when the forest was free
- Others emphasise [[Harfalene Wythern]]'s discovery of [[Haligdene]] in the 13th century, seeing him as the true founder
- Still others suggest they are the same person somehow, or that the later Harfalene fulfilled the ancient pattern
- A few versions whisper that every generation produces a Greenfinger — someone whose hands bring life to what they touch

This multiplicity is not seen as contradiction but as richness — each version true in its own way.

## Seasonal Gatherings

Four times a year, at the turning of seasons, forest-folk gather at [[Greenweft]] for the sharing of knowledge, settling of disputes, and arrangement of marriages between family groups. The Eldest Stewards hold informal authority during these gatherings, though decisions are made by consensus rather than decree.

The **Midwinter Gathering** — three days before the [[The Midwinter Tribute|Midwinter Tribute]] — is the largest and most significant.

**See Also:** [[Harfalene Greenfinger]] · [[Harfalene Wythern]] · [[The Wytherns]] · [[Greenweft]]
